title: Javascript ES6 - Import, Export and Modules
summary: A focused look at ES6 modules: default exports, named exports, the matching import syntax, wildcard imports, and how this differs from Node's require. Demonstrated with a math.js module exporting pi, doublePi and triplePi into a React list.

concepts.heading: Modules in general
points: Any JavaScript file can be a module: it keeps its contents private unless it exports them, and other files pull in only what they need.
This is the mechanism behind import React from "react" and behind splitting React components across files; it is not React-specific.
math.js here is a plain JS file, not a component, so it uses the .js extension.

concepts.heading: Default export
points: export default pi; exposes one main value. A file can have at most one default export.
The importer chooses the local name: import pi from "./math.js" or import PI from "./math.js" both receive the same value, as long as the code then uses the same name consistently.
The extension in the path is optional with bundlers like Babel/Vite; it was kept in the demo for visibility.

concepts.heading: Named exports
points: Additional exports go in a braces list: export { doublePi, triplePi };. A file can have any number of these.
Import them with braces after the default import, separated by a comma: import PI, { doublePi, triplePi } from "./math.js";.
Names inside the braces must exactly match the exported names; renaming on import requires the 'as' keyword (import { doublePi as double }). (Extra)
Exported functions are imported as functions: to display a result in JSX, call it, e.g. {doublePi()}.

concepts.heading: Wildcard import
points: import * as pi from "./math.js"; collects every export into one namespace object, which must be given a name.
The object has the named functions as properties (pi.doublePi(), pi.triplePi()) and the default export under the property default (pi.default).
Style guides tend to discourage this: it hides which things are really used and loses the clarity of a clear default plus specific named imports.

concepts.heading: ES6 import/export versus Node require
points: Before ES6 modules, Node code used const x = require("x"). require is a Node feature, not part of the JavaScript language, and it does not work in browsers directly.

At the time of the lecture, browser support for ES6 modules was incomplete; Babel (compiling to older syntax) made ES6 safe in React apps. (Extra) Today all modern browsers support ES modules natively.
The instructor prefers import/export syntax for its clarity.

pitfalls: Putting more than one export default in a file is a syntax error.
Named imports are case-sensitive and must match the export; a typo yields undefined or a missing-export error.
Writing {doublePi} instead of {doublePi()} in JSX tries to render the function itself rather than its result.
Omitting curly braces around named imports imports the default export instead.
